topics.name: Arrays
topics.unit: Complex Data Types notes / Exam cheat sheet

topics.name: Classes with dynamic data (Rule of Three)

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the primitive data types listed in the Basics Review notes?
questions.explain: The primitive types are short, int, long, float, double, long double, bool and char. string is a complex type that comes from the string library. char is tempting to rule out because it holds text, but it is a primitive single-character type.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.code:
int a = 7, b = 2;
cout << a / b << " " << a % b;
questions.explain: Both operands are int, so 7 / 2 truncates to 3, and 7 % 2 is the remainder 1. 3.5 is the trap: integer division never produces a fractional result.

questions.q: What value does d hold after this line runs?
questions.code: double d = 1 / 2 * 10.0;
questions.explain: Evaluation goes left to right: 1 / 2 is integer division and gives 0, and 0 * 10.0 is 0.0. Getting 5 requires writing 1.0 / 2 or 0.5 so the division happens in floating point.

questions.q: What value is stored in x?
questions.explain: * and % share a precedence level higher than +, and they are evaluated left to right: 3 * 4 = 12, then 12 % 5 = 2, then 2 + 2 = 4. You get 0 only if you add first, (2 + 3) * 4 % 5.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: static_cast<int> truncates and drops the fractional part. It does not round, so 19.99 becomes 19, not 20.

questions.q: Which condition is true exactly when x is strictly between 10 and 20?
questions.explain: Two relational tests must be joined with &&. The chained form 10 < x < 20 compiles, but it evaluates (10 < x) to 0 or 1 first and then compares that to 20, so it is always true. Using || is also always true.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.code:
bool b = !true || 5 > 3 && 2 == 3;
cout << b;
questions.explain: ! comes first, so !true is false. Next, 5 > 3 is true and 2 == 3 is false, and && binds tighter than ||: true && false gives false. Then false || false is false. cout prints a bool as 0 or 1 by default, so the output is 0, not the word false.

questions.q: What does this code print? (Spaces are shown as _ )
questions.code: cout << setw(5) << 42 << setw(3) << 7 << endl;
questions.explain: setw(n) right-justifies only the next value in a field n characters wide. 42 is padded to 5 characters (3 spaces), and 7 is padded to 3 characters (2 spaces). The values are not left-justified by default.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.code:
cout << fixed << setprecision(2);
cout << 3.14159 << " " << 20.0 / 8;
questions.explain: fixed with setprecision(2) is sticky and always shows exactly 2 digits after the decimal point. 20.0 / 8 is 2.5, which prints as 2.50. Without fixed you would see 2.5.

questions.q: What happens with this code?
questions.code:
const double TAX_RATE = 0.0675;
TAX_RATE = 0.07;
choices: The compiler warns, and TAX_RATE quietly stays 0.0675
It does not compile because TAX_RATE is a named constant
questions.explain: A const variable cannot be changed after it is initialized, so the assignment is a compile-time error. It is not just a warning, and it is not something that fails at runtime.

questions.q: Which of these is a character literal?
questions.explain: Character literals use single quotes. "z" in double quotes is a string literal, 7.71e-5 is a floating-point literal, and true is a boolean literal.

questions.q: Suppose a starts as 5 and b as 3. What does this code print?
questions.explain: First a = 5 * 2 - 3 = 7. Then b = 7 % 5 + 3 = 2 + 3 = 5. b is computed from the new a, and 7 2 comes from forgetting to add b back in.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: number / 4 is int / int, so it truncates to 2 before the result is converted to double. A double holding 2.0 prints as 2. To get 2.5, write number / 4.0.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: In C++ the result of % takes the sign of the left operand: -7 = 3 * (-2) + (-1), so the remainder is -1. The answer 2 is what mathematical modulo would give, but C++ does not work that way.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: With x == 2, execution jumps to case 2 and prints B. That case has no break, so it falls through into case 3, prints C, and then reaches break. The answer B would only be right if every case ended with a break.

questions.q: Which type CANNOT be used as the controlling expression of a switch statement?
questions.explain: switch works with integer types, char and enumerations. It does not work with floating-point types or strings. char is allowed because it is an integer type underneath.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: A do-while loop always runs its body once before it checks the condition, so 10 is printed. Then i becomes 11, the test 11 < 5 is false, and the loop stops. A while loop would print nothing here.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: n goes 1 -> 3 -> 9 -> 27 -> 81, which is 4 iterations. The condition is checked before each pass, so n = 27 (still < 50) gets one more multiplication. Stopping at 3 27 is an off-by-one in the trace.

questions.q: What does this code print? (spaces shown as _ )
questions.explain: On row i the inner loop prints 1 up to i, and each row ends with a space. The trap 1 22 333 comes from printing i instead of j.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: An else pairs with the nearest unmatched if, whatever the indentation suggests. 12 % 4 == 0 is true, 12 % 5 == 0 is false, so the inner if's else runs and prints B. The indentation makes it look like the else belongs to the outer if, which would print nothing.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: x = 5 is an assignment, not a comparison. It stores 5 in x and evaluates to 5, which is nonzero and therefore true. So it prints five, and x is now 5. The comparison operator is ==.

questions.q: This loop should add up only the odd numbers entered, stopping when 0 is entered. Which pair of blanks is correct?
questions.explain: The loop runs until the sentinel 0 is entered, and a number is odd when number % 2 != 0. Testing for != 0 also handles negative odd numbers, where % 2 gives -1. That is why number % 2 == 1 and number > 0 are wrong.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: Multiples of 3 (0, 3, 6) are skipped by continue. At i = 8 the continue test is false (8 % 3 is 2), and then 8 > 7 triggers break before anything is printed. So 8 never appears.

questions.q: What happens when this code runs?
questions.explain: Without braces, only the first statement (cout << i;) belongs to the while loop. i++ is outside the loop and never runs, so i stays 0 and the condition is always true. The indentation is misleading.

questions.q: What does this calculator code print when cOperator is '/'?
questions.explain: The '/' case sets result = 5 / 12 = 0, but it has no break, so it falls through into the '%' case and overwrites result with 5 % 12 = 5. The answer 0 ignores the fall-through.

questions.q: How many times does count++ execute?
questions.explain: i takes the values 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, which is 6 values, because <= includes 5. Answering 5 is the classic off-by-one mistake.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: x goes 0, 3, 6, 9, 12. When x is 9 the test 9 < 10 is still true, so 3 is added once more, giving 12. The loop does not stop at 10.

questions.q: What happens when you compile this program?
choices: It compiles, then crashes at runtime
Compile error: 'displayHelloWorld' was not declared in this scope
questions.explain: The compiler reads from top to bottom, and main calls the function before the compiler has seen any declaration of it. You fix this by adding a prototype above main or by moving the definition up.

questions.q: A function is defined later in the file as double area(double l, double w) { ... }. Which line is a valid prototype for it?
questions.explain: A prototype gives the return type, the name and the parameter types, and it ends with a semicolon. Parameter names are optional. A prototype with no semicolon is just the start of a function definition.

questions.q: Given void addNumbers(int iX, int iY = 10), which call is INVALID?
questions.explain: iX has no default value, so the caller must always supply at least one argument. addNumbers(5 + 1) is fine because an argument can be any expression.

questions.q: Which function header is ILLEGAL?
choices: void f(int a, int b = 2, int c = 3);
questions.explain: Default parameters must be given from right to left. Once a parameter has a default, every parameter after it needs one too, and here b follows a defaulted parameter but has no default.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: Arguments fill parameters from the left, and any missing ones use their defaults. volume(4) is 4*2*3 = 24, volume(4,5) is 4*5*3 = 60, and volume(4,5,6) is 120.

questions.q: Which pair of functions CANNOT both exist in the same program?
choices: int f(int x);  and  double f(int x);
void f(string s);  and  void f(char c);
int f(int x);  and  int f(double x);
int f(int x);  and  int f(int x, int y);
questions.explain: Overloads must have different parameter lists, and a different return type alone is not enough. The compiler could not tell which f(5) you meant.

questions.q: What does this code print?
choices: It fails to compile because of ambiguity
questions.explain: The compiler picks the overload whose parameter type best matches each argument. 3 is an int, 3.0 is a double, and string("3") is a string. There is no ambiguity because each call has an exact match.

questions.q: What is wrong with this function?
choices: It compiles, but the value it returns is always 0
It produces a warning only, and the return is ignored
A void function cannot return a value, so it does not compile
Nothing. It returns dArea to the caller
questions.explain: A void function returns no data. return dArea; there is a compile error (return-statement with a value, in function returning 'void'). To fix it, change the return type to double.

questions.q: This function is missing its return statement. What happens when it is called?
choices: The returned value is undefined. It might look correct by accident, and -Wreturn-type can warn about it
The compiler refuses to build the program
questions.explain: If a value-returning function reaches its end without a return, the result is undefined, and sometimes it happens to be the right number. A compiler warning (-Wreturn-type, part of -Wall) can catch this. Because it is usually a warning and not an error, thinking the build always fails is the tempting mistake.

questions.q: Which assert fails first?
questions.explain: The function subtracts inches when it should add them. Lines A and B pass inches = 0, so the bug does not show. Line C computes 0*12 - 3 = -3, not 3, so the assertion fails and the program aborts there. Line D would pass.

questions.q: In the course's function documentation header, what does labeling a parameter I/O mean?
choices: It is only read and never changed
It comes in with data, and the function modifies that data
It is a file stream used for input or output
It starts with no data and is only used to send a result out
questions.explain: I means passed in and not modified. O means used only to pass data out. I/O means passed in with data that the function changes. The file-stream reading is a guess based on the letters and does not reflect what the label means.

questions.q: When main calls displayHelloWorld(), what happens on the call stack?
choices: Nothing happens on the stack, because only variables live there, not function calls
main's frame is removed and replaced by displayHelloWorld's frame
A new stack frame for displayHelloWorld (its parameters, locals and return address) is pushed on top of main's frame and popped when it returns
A frame is added to the bottom of the stack, below main
questions.explain: Each call pushes a frame onto the top of the stack, and returning pops it so control goes back to main. main's frame stays underneath the whole time; it is never replaced.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: mystery(3, 8): 3 > 8 is false, so it returns 8 - 3 + 1 = 6. mystery(8, 3): 8 > 3 is true, so it returns 5 and exits immediately. The second return line never runs for that call.

questions.q: In this call from main, displayMovie(szMovie, dRating); what are szMovie and dRating?
choices: Arguments: values supplied in the function call
Parameters: variables declared in the function definition
questions.explain: Arguments are what you pass at the call site. Parameters are the variables listed in the function's definition, and they receive copies of (or references to) the arguments. People often mix the two words up.

questions.q: displayMovie is defined as void displayMovie(string szMovie, double dRating). What happens with the call displayMovie(dRating, szMovie); ?
choices: It runs and prints the values in reverse order
Compile error: the arguments are in the wrong order, and a double cannot be converted to a string
It compiles, but szMovie becomes an empty string
It works, because C++ matches arguments to parameters by name
questions.explain: Arguments are matched to parameters by position, not by name. The first parameter expects a string, and a double cannot be converted to one, so the compiler rejects the call.

questions.q: What does this program print?
questions.explain: Pass by value gives the function its own copies. It changes and prints the copies (6 7), and main's a and b remain 1 and 2.

questions.q: After this "swap" call, what are iX and iY in main?
questions.explain: Only iA is a reference. iA = iB copies 9 into iX. iB is a copy, so changing it does not affect iY, which stays 9. Both end up as 9, so this is not a working swap; the & is missing on iB.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: x is passed by value, so doubling it changes only the copy, and a stays 3. y is a reference to b, so b becomes 10.

questions.q: Why do the notes recommend passing a large string to a function by reference?
choices: Strings cannot be passed by value in C++
Pass by reference makes the function run in constant time
It avoids copying the whole string, and it lets the function modify the caller's string if needed
References make the string read-only automatically
questions.explain: Pass by value copies every character, while a reference just aliases the original. Strings can be passed by value; it is only less efficient. To prevent modification you would add const, which a plain reference does not do.

questions.q: What does this program print?
questions.explain: The x inside f is a separate local variable that hides the global x, so x++ changes only the local copy. main prints the global x, which is still 5.

questions.q: What does this program print?
questions.explain: inc() always increments the global count, which ends at 3. When main prints count, its local count (7) hides the global one, so 7 is printed. Answering 8 assumes inc() changed the local variable.

questions.q: What happens with this code?
choices: Compile error: sq is not declared in this scope
questions.explain: sq is declared inside the loop body's block, so it stops existing when that block ends. Using it after the loop is a scope error that the compiler catches; it is not something that happens at runtime.

questions.q: Given void doubleIt(int& n) { n *= 2; }, what happens with the call doubleIt(5); ?
choices: It compiles, and the call does nothing
Compile error: a non-const reference must refer to a variable, not a literal
questions.explain: A non-const reference parameter must bind to a variable whose memory the function can modify. A literal such as 5 has no such memory, so the compiler rejects the call.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: s is passed by value, so the function uppercases its own copy. To change w, the parameter would need to be string& s.

questions.q: A function must give back both a quotient and a remainder. Which header follows the course's approach?
choices: int, int divide(int a, int b)
int divide(int a, int b, int q, int r)
void divide(int a, int b, int& q, int& r)
void divide(int a, int b, int q, int r)
questions.explain: A return statement can send back only one value, so the extra results go out through reference parameters (documented as O). Value parameters q and r would be local copies that the caller never sees.

questions.q: Where can a function's parameters be used?
choices: In main and the function itself
Anywhere in the program after the function is called
questions.explain: Parameters have function scope. They are created when the function is called and destroyed when it returns.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: r is another name for a. r += 3 makes a = 8, then a *= 2 makes it 16. Reading r reads the same memory, so it is also 16.

questions.q: In void countWords(ifstream& fin, int& iCount), iCount holds no meaningful value when the function is called, and the function stores the result in it. How should iCount be labeled in the doc header?
choices: It needs no label because it is a reference
questions.explain: O means the parameter is used only to pass data out. I/O would be correct only if the function also used the value that came in. Every parameter gets a label, including references.

questions.q: How many bytes are needed to store the characters of "Hello World", including the null byte?
questions.explain: "Hello World" has 11 characters (the space counts), plus 1 for the terminating null byte, for 12 in total. Answering 11 forgets the \0.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.code:
string s = "Toy Story";
cout << s.size();
questions.explain: size() returns the number of characters, including the space but not the null terminator: T-o-y-space-S-t-o-r-y is 9. The answer 10 is the storage count that includes \0.

questions.q: What happens when this code runs?
questions.code:
string szMovie = "Toy story";
char cLetter = szMovie.at(11);
choices: cLetter gets a random garbage value
It throws a std::out_of_range exception, which terminates the program
questions.explain: at() is bounds-checked. Index 11 is not less than size() (9), so it throws out_of_range. The garbage-value outcome is what can happen with unchecked [] access.

questions.q: Why do the notes call szMovie[11] the "bad way" when szMovie is "Toy story"?
choices: [] cannot be used with strings at all
[] does no bounds checking, so an out-of-range index silently reads garbage (undefined behavior)
questions.explain: Square-bracket access trusts the index, so going past the end is undefined behavior and does not produce a clean error. at() checks the index and throws instead.

questions.q: What does the expression evaluate to?
questions.code:
string code = "mx42";
code.at(0) >= 65 && code.at(0) <= 90
choices: It does not compile, because you cannot compare a char to an int
false, because 'm' is ASCII 109, outside the uppercase range 65-90
questions.explain: Characters compare by their ASCII codes. Uppercase letters are 65-90, and lowercase 'm' is 109, so the second test fails. Comparing a char with an int is perfectly legal.

questions.q: The user types 20, presses Enter, then types Sam Lee and presses Enter. What does name contain?
questions.explain: cin >> age leaves the newline in the input buffer. getline then reads up to that newline right away and gets an empty string. Calling cin.ignore() before getline fixes this.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: The >> operator on an istringstream pulls whitespace-separated tokens in order: n = 42, a = "apples", b = "and". The code prints b followed by n.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.code:
string s = "banana";
cout << s.find("na");
questions.explain: find returns the 0-based index where the first match starts. In b-a-n-a-n-a, "na" first begins at index 2. The answer 4 is the second occurrence.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: "Ada" (3) + " " (1) + "Lovelace" (8) = 12, and += "!" adds 1 more, giving 13. size() never counts the null byte.

questions.q: This loop is meant to print the characters at even indices of movie. With movie = "Jaws", what happens?
questions.code:
for (int i = 0; i <= movie.length(); i = i + 2)
    cout << movie.at(i);
choices: It prints Jw, then at(4) throws out_of_range
questions.explain: i takes the values 0, 2, 4. Because the condition uses <=, i = 4 is allowed, but the valid indices are only 0-3. The fix is i < movie.length().

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: The digit characters in "R2-D2 & C-3PO" are 2, 2 and 3, so the count is 3. The answer 13 is the string's total length.

questions.q: Which statement about the null byte at the end of a string is correct?
choices: It is a space character, ASCII 32
It is included in the value returned by size()
Its ASCII value is 0. It is not the character '0', which is ASCII 48
questions.explain: The terminator \0 has numeric value 0. The digit character '0' is a different character, with code 48, and size() does not count the terminator.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: 'D' is 68, and adding 32 gives 100, which is 'd'. Because c is a char, cout prints the character, not the number.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: i takes the values 1, 3, 5, so the sum is scores[1] + scores[3] + scores[5] = 5 + 9 + 13 = 27. The answer 21 comes from starting at index 0 (3 + 7 + 11).

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: In a partially initialized array, the elements that are not listed are set to 0. So b[2] is 0 and b[1] is 2, which gives 2.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: An array argument is passed as the address of its first element, so the function works on the caller's actual array. That is why arrays behave as if passed by reference.

questions.q: Why do functions that take an array parameter almost always take a separate size parameter too?
choices: Without the size, the function would get a copy of only the first element
The size makes the array be passed by value
C++ requires every array parameter to be followed by an int
Inside the function the array parameter is really just a pointer to the first element, so the function cannot tell how many elements there are
questions.explain: The array decays to a pointer, so the length information is lost. You must pass the size yourself, or the loops cannot know where to stop.

questions.q: What is the problem with this code?
choices: Index 5 is out of bounds (valid indices are 0-4). C++ does not check it, so this is undefined behavior
It does not compile, because the compiler checks array bounds
Nothing. It quietly grows the array to 6 elements
questions.explain: Built-in arrays have no bounds checking, so the write lands in memory the array does not own. It usually compiles without complaint, and neither throwing nor resizing ever happens with a raw array.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: idx tracks the position of the largest value. a[2] = 9 becomes the max, and the comparison at a[3] is 9 > 9, which is false, so idx stays 2. Printing 9 would be printing the value, not the index.

questions.q: For double temps[8], what is the range of valid indices?
questions.explain: Arrays are 0-indexed, so an 8-element array has indices 0 through size - 1 = 7.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: i starts at 3 and goes down by 2, visiting indices 3 and 1, which print a[3] = 4 and a[1] = 2. The answer 31 confuses indices with values.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: Each element becomes itself plus the already-updated previous element (a running total): 1, 3, 6, 10, 15. The answer 9 would come from using the original a[3] = 4.

questions.q: What happens with the last line?
choices: b becomes an alias for a
Compile error: you cannot assign one whole array to another
b becomes a copy of a
questions.explain: An array name is a constant pointer to its first element and cannot be assigned to. To copy an array you need a loop that copies each element.

questions.q: Given Student roster[30]; where Student has a dGPA member, how do you access the GPA of the third student?
questions.explain: First index the array to get one Student (index 2 is the third), then use the dot operator on it. roster[3] is off by one.

questions.q: What does the const in this parameter do?
questions.code: int sumArray(const int arr[], int n);
choices: It makes the function copy the array
It makes the array's size fixed
It stops the function from modifying the array's elements. arr[0] = 1; inside it would not compile
questions.explain: const int arr[] means the elements are read-only inside the function. It documents intent and protects the caller's data. It does not affect the separate parameter n.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: The loop counts how many elements equal a[0] (which is 2), and a[0] counts itself: indices 0, 2 and 4, so 3. Answering 2 forgets that a[0] matches itself.

questions.q: In struct Student { string szName; int iID; };, what is the name Student called?
questions.explain: A structure has a tag (its name) and data members (the items inside it, such as szName and iID).

questions.q: Why does this code fail to compile?
choices: The struct definition is missing the semicolon after its closing brace
questions.explain: A struct (or class) definition must end with };. Leaving out that semicolon is one of the most common beginner compile errors.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: A partial initializer list fills members in order. Members that are not listed keep their default values from the struct definition, so qty = 1 and weight = 0.5.

questions.q: Student's first member is szStudentID and its fifth member is szMajor. What does Student s = {"Computer Science"}; do?
choices: It compiles, but "Computer Science" goes into the first member, szStudentID
It stores "Computer Science" in szMajor because the types match
It sets every string member to "Computer Science"
questions.explain: Initializer values are assigned strictly in member order, and you cannot skip members. Because the types match, the code compiles, but the value ends up in the wrong member.

questions.q: What happens with cout << studentA; where studentA is a struct Student?
choices: It prints the struct's memory address
It prints only the first member
Compile error: there is no operator<< that knows how to print a Student
It prints every member separated by spaces
questions.explain: C++ has no built-in way to print a whole struct. You either print each member yourself or overload operator<<.

questions.q: Given these structs and Person p;, which expression is p's zip code?
questions.code:
struct Address { string city; int zip; };
struct Person  { string name; Address home; };
questions.explain: Chain the dot operator through the nested member: p, then its home member (an Address), then zip. You use the member's name (home), not the type name (Address).

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: Assigning one struct to another copies every member, so b is independent of a. Changing b.x does not affect a.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: The struct is passed by value, so grow doubles a copy. To change a, the parameter should be Point& p.

questions.q: Why does *pp.y = 9; fail when pp is a Point*?
choices: pp must first be converted to a reference
You cannot change a struct through a pointer
* must come after the member name
The dot operator binds tighter than *, so this means *(pp.y), and a pointer has no member y
questions.explain: Because of precedence, pp.y is evaluated first, which is invalid on a pointer. Write (*pp).y = 9; or, more simply, pp->y = 9;.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: Only songs with more than 6 plays are added: B (12) and C (8), giving 20. A with 5 plays is skipped. The answer 2 counts the matching songs instead of summing their plays.

questions.q: According to the Classes notes, what is a downside of using a struct to group data?
choices: There is no way to restrict who can modify its data members
Struct members cannot have default values
Structs cannot be nested inside other structs
questions.explain: Every member of a plain struct can be read and changed by any code, so it gives no encapsulation. Classes fix this with private members. The other options are false: structs can hold strings, have default values and be nested.

questions.q: What happens with this code?
choices: Compile error: == is not defined for Point unless you overload it
It prints different, because they are separate objects
It compares only the first members
questions.explain: C++ does not generate comparison operators for structs. You either compare the members yourself or write an operator== overload.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: dGPA has a default value in the struct definition, so any Student created without an initializer for it starts with 4. Members without defaults, such as lCreditHours in other examples, are a different case.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: p first points to a: *p = 3 + 7 stores 10 in a. Then p is moved to b, and *p = 7 * 2 stores 14 in b.

questions.q: Given int iX = 10; int* pi = &iX;, what does cout << π print?
choices: The address of the pointer variable pi itself
The address of the address of iX, which is always 0
questions.explain: pi holds iX's address, and *pi is 10. &pi is where pi itself is stored in memory, which is a different location. Saying it prints iX's address confuses pi with &pi.

questions.q: What is wrong with this code?
questions.code:
int* p;
*p = 5;
choices: p is uninitialized, so writing through it is undefined behavior
It does not compile, because pointers cannot be dereferenced
p automatically points to nullptr, so this safely does nothing
Nothing. It stores 5 in a new int

questions.q: Which statement about references and pointers is TRUE?

A reference can later be changed to refer to a different variable

questions.q: Where does memory created with new come from?
questions.explain: new allocates anonymous memory on the heap while the program runs. Ordinary local variables live on the stack, and their sizes are fixed when the program is compiled.

questions.q: Which allocation is guaranteed to start with the value 0?

questions.q: What is wrong with this code?

p is a dangling pointer on the second line

questions.q: Given double* d = new double[n];, how should the memory be released?

questions.q: Which command runs a program under Valgrind with full leak checking?
questions.explain: Valgrind is a separate tool that wraps the running executable and reports leaks, use of uninitialized memory, out-of-bounds access and double deletes. -Wall is a g++ warning flag, not a Valgrind option.

questions.q: Why is it good practice to write p = nullptr; right after delete p; ?
choices: delete does not actually free the memory until p is set to nullptr
It prevents accidental use of a dangling pointer, because the null value can be checked, and deleting nullptr again is harmless
It makes the delete happen automatically at the end of scope
It returns the memory to the operating system faster
questions.explain: The memory is freed by delete itself. Setting the pointer to nullptr just marks it as not pointing anywhere, so later null checks work and an accidental second delete does nothing.

questions.q: What is wrong with this code?

Nothing. It frees x's memory early
x was not allocated with new, so deleting it is undefined behavior
questions.explain: delete may be used only on memory that came from new. x is a stack variable, and the system cleans it up automatically.

questions.q: This growth logic is from the inventory program. What does it print?

questions.explain: 1 * 0.5 = 0.5, and static_cast<int> truncates that to 0, so newCapacity starts at 1. The guard sees that 1 <= 1 and bumps it to 2. Without the guard the array would never grow.

questions.q: This function doubles a dynamic array's capacity. What is the bug?

The old array is never deleted, so it leaks
bigger should be declared as a reference

questions.q: In the inventory program, resizeInventory takes Item*& inventory. What would go wrong if the parameter were just Item* inventory and the function did delete[] inventory; inventory = newInventory;?
choices: The caller's pointer would still hold the old, now-deleted address (a dangling pointer), and the new array would leak
It would not compile, because pointers cannot be parameters

The new array would be deleted instead of the old one

questions.q: A class holds a char* allocated with new[] and relies on the compiler-provided copy constructor. What goes wrong when an object is copied?
choices: The copy gets a nullptr instead of the buffer
The compiler refuses to copy objects that contain pointers
The buffer is deep-copied automatically, so nothing goes wrong
Only the pointer is copied (a shallow copy), so both objects share one buffer, and the second destructor deletes it again
questions.explain: The default copy constructor copies each member as it is, so the copy gets the same address. Changes through one object show up in the other, and when both destructors call delete[] on the same block you get a double deletion.

questions.q: According to the Rule of Three, a class that needs a custom destructor probably also needs which two members?
choices: A copy constructor and a copy assignment operator
A static counter and a private helper
A default constructor and a getter
A move constructor and a move assignment operator
questions.explain: The three are the destructor, the copy constructor and operator=. All of them deal with owning dynamic memory. Move operations are what the Rule of Five adds on top.

questions.q: Why does the assignment operator check if (this != &other) before doing anything?
choices: For a = a, it would otherwise delete[] its own data and then try to copy from the memory it just freed
To make the assignment run faster when the objects are different
Because this is a nullptr when the object is first being assigned
To avoid comparing two different classes

questions.q: Why does operator= end with return *this; and return SimpleString& ?

Returning is required to free the old memory
It returns the other object so the caller can check it

questions.q: Why must a copy constructor take its parameter by reference, as in Student(const Student& other), and not by value?
choices: Passing by value would itself require a copy, which calls the copy constructor again, leading to infinite recursion
By value would make the copy read-only
The compiler only allows references to classes
References are faster, but by value would also work
questions.explain: Making a by-value parameter means copying the argument, and copying is exactly what the copy constructor does, so it would call itself forever. const prevents accidental changes to the source.

questions.q: A class allocates an array with new[] in its constructor but has no destructor. What happens each time an object goes out of scope?
choices: The array is moved to the stack
The object's members are destroyed, but the heap array they pointed to is never freed, so memory leaks
The compiler-generated destructor calls delete[] automatically
questions.explain: The default destructor destroys the pointer member itself but never frees what it points to. You need ~ClassName() { delete[] ptr; } to release it.

questions.q: In this constructor, why is the buffer allocated with strlen(str) + 1 characters?

strlen counts from 1, so +1 corrects for that
To leave space for one more character to be appended later

questions.q: Which special member function runs on Line 3 and on Line 4?

Line 3: assignment operator. Line 4: copy constructor
questions.explain: Line 3 creates a new object from an existing one, which is copy construction, even though it uses =. Line 4 assigns to an object that already exists, so operator= runs.

questions.q: If SimpleString's operator= left out the line delete[] pszData;, what would happen on b = a;?

b and a would share a buffer
Nothing, because the destructor frees the old buffer later

questions.q: The Rule of Five (C++11) adds which two functions to the Rule of Three?
choices: The move constructor and the move assignment operator
The default constructor and the destructor
questions.explain: Move operations let temporary objects hand over their dynamic memory instead of having it copied. Together with the destructor, copy constructor and copy assignment, that makes five.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a class compared with an object?

A class and an object are the same thing

An object is a blueprint, and a class is an instance

questions.q: Which statement about constructors is FALSE?

A constructor runs automatically when an object is created

questions.q: A class declares static int iStudentCount; but the line int Student::iStudentCount = 0; is missing. What happens?

iStudentCount is automatically created and set to 0

Each object gets its own iStudentCount

questions.q: Why does this member function fail to compile?

Static functions must be defined outside the class

questions.q: In void Student::displayStudent() { ... }, what is the :: operator called?

questions.q: What does : szName(szN), iGrade(iG) do in this constructor?

It declares two new local variables
It is a member initializer list that initializes the members directly with the parameter values before the body runs

questions.q: When is the destructor of a local (stack) object called?

Only when the programmer calls it explicitly
Only when the whole program exits
questions.explain: C++ destroys local objects automatically at the closing brace of the block they were declared in. The notes say destructors are never called manually.

questions.q: This class defines only a parameterized constructor. What happens with Student s; ?

questions.q: Given a Student class whose default constructor prints *, what does Student roster[3]; print?

A member function whose body is written directly inside the class definition
A member function defined outside the class with ::

questions.q: Why should getter functions be marked const, as in string getName() const?

It promises the function will not modify the object, and it allows the getter to be called on const objects or through const references

The name of the current function

questions.q: isValidGrade is declared in the private section of Student. Which code can call it?

questions.q: What is the main benefit of making data members private and exposing setters?

Setters make the program run faster
It lets outside code change the members directly

questions.q: A class has a public mutator setAge(int a) and an accessor getAge() const. Which description is correct?

questions.q: Why should a file stream be passed to a function by reference, as in void readAll(ifstream& fin)?

questions.q: Why is a loop of the form while (!fin.eof()) { fin >> n; sum += n; } risky?
choices: eof() cannot be used with ifstream
eof() becomes true only after a read has tried to go past the end, so if trailing whitespace remains, the loop runs one extra time after a failed read
eof() always returns true on the first call
questions.explain: After the last number, a newline is usually still waiting to be read, so eof() is still false. The next >> fails, and the body still adds n. Testing the read itself, with while (fin >> n), avoids this.

questions.q: A program opens result.txt with an ofstream and writes the line Result is 110. You run the program twice. What does result.txt contain?
choices: Nothing, because the second run fails to open an existing file
Result is 110Result is 110 on one line
questions.explain: An ofstream opened without ios::app truncates the existing file, so each run overwrites the last one. Getting two lines would require append mode.

questions.q: Which statement correctly closes an open ifstream named fin?
questions.explain: close is a member function that takes no arguments, because the stream already knows which file it has open. Leaving off the () does not call it.

questions.q: people.txt contains the text below. How many times does the loop body run?
questions.explain: The file stores the number first, but the code reads the name first. name reads "85" without trouble, since a string accepts any token, but score then tries to read "Alice" as an int, which fails. The condition is false right away. This is the reading-in-the-wrong-order mistake.

questions.q: Right after fin.open("input.txt");, which check correctly detects that the open failed?
questions.explain: fail() returns true when an operation, including open, has failed. if (!fin) is equivalent. good() is true when things are fine, the opposite of what we want to detect, and eof() is about reaching the end of the data.

questions.q: Using linear search on {5, 9, 3, 7, 2}, how many comparisons are made to find the target 2?
questions.explain: Linear search checks indices 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 in order, and 2 is in the last slot, so all 5 elements are compared. This is the worst case.

questions.q: What does the course's linearSearch return when the target is not in the array?
choices: The index of the closest value
questions.explain: -1 can never be a valid index, so it signals not found. Returning 0 would be confused with finding the target at index 0.

questions.q: What requirement must be met before binary search can be used on an array?
choices: The array must contain no duplicates
The array must have an even number of elements
The array must be dynamically allocated
questions.explain: Binary search throws away half of the range based on comparisons, which only works if the order is known. Odd or even size and duplicates do not matter.

questions.q: Using the course's binarySearch on {2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14} with target 4, which indices are checked as mid?
questions.explain: low = 0 and high = 6, so mid = 3 (value 8). 4 < 8, so high = 2. Next, mid = (0 + 2) / 2 = 1 (value 4), a match. Starting from index 0 describes linear search.

questions.q: Using the binarySearch from the notes on {1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11} with target 6, what are low and high when the loop ends?
questions.explain: Step 1: mid = 2 (value 5), 6 > 5, so low = 3. Step 2: mid = 4 (value 9), 6 < 9, so high = 3. Step 3: mid = 3 (value 7), 6 < 7, so high = 2. Now low > high, the loop exits, and the function returns -1.

questions.q: What does binarySearch return for target 9 on the UNSORTED array {9, 2, 7, 4, 1}?
questions.explain: mid = 2 (value 7): 9 > 7, so the search moves right (low = 3). mid = 3 (value 4) moves right again, then mid = 4 (value 1), then low = 5 > high, so the loop exits. The left side, where 9 actually is, gets discarded. That is why sorting is required.

questions.q: To make binary search work on an array sorted in DESCENDING order, what must change?
choices: Nothing. Binary search works the same in either order
Start mid at the last index
Reverse the direction: if the target is greater than the middle value, search the LEFT half (high = mid - 1)
questions.explain: In descending order, larger values are on the left, so the comparison that picks the half has to be flipped. The loop structure stays the same.

questions.q: You need to look up one value, once, in a small unsorted array. Which approach do the notes recommend?
questions.explain: Sorting costs at least O(n log n), more than one O(n) scan. Binary search pays off when the data is already sorted and you will search it many times.

questions.q: About how many comparisons does binary search need in the worst case on a sorted array of 1024 elements?
questions.explain: Each step halves the range, and log2(1024) = 10, so it takes roughly 10 or 11 steps. The answer 512 assumes each step removes only one element at a time.

questions.q: What is linear search's best case, and when does it happen?
choices: O(1), when the target is the first element
O(1), when the target is the last element
O(n), always, because it scans the whole array
O(log n), when the array is sorted
questions.explain: If the very first comparison matches, the search returns immediately. The worst case, O(n), happens when the target is last or missing.

questions.q: What does this code print?
questions.explain: The function does not return early. It keeps overwriting pos with every match, so it returns the LAST index holding 4, which is index 4. The answer 3 is the number of matches.

questions.q: A student writes iLow = iMid; instead of iLow = iMid + 1; in binary search. What can happen when searching {1, 3} for 3?
choices: It works correctly, just more slowly
An infinite loop: mid stays 0, so low never moves past it
questions.explain: low = 0 and high = 1 give mid = 0 (value 1). 3 > 1 sets low = mid = 0 again, so nothing changes and the loop never ends. The +1 is what guarantees the range shrinks.

questions.q: Which condition completes this linear search through an array of Student structs by ID?
questions.explain: Index the array to get one Student, then compare its iID field with the target. Comparing a whole struct to an int does not compile.

questions.q: Ascending selection sort is run on [8, 3, 6, 1, 5]. What does the array look like after the first pass (i = 0)?
questions.explain: The first pass finds the minimum (1, at index 3) and swaps it with index 0, so 8 moves to where 1 was. Shifting everything right, as in [1, 8, 3, 6, 5], is what insertion sort does.

questions.q: Continuing ascending selection sort on [8, 3, 6, 1, 5], what does the array look like after THREE passes (i = 0, 1, 2)?
questions.explain: Pass 0 gives [1, 3, 6, 8, 5]. Pass 1 finds that 3 is already the minimum, so it swaps index 1 with itself. Pass 2 finds 5 at index 4 and swaps it with 6, giving [1, 3, 5, 8, 6]. One more pass is needed to finish.

questions.q: Ascending insertion sort is run on [4, 1, 3, 9, 2]. What does the array look like after the pass with i = 2?
questions.explain: i = 1 inserts 1, giving [1, 4, 3, 9, 2]. i = 2 takes key 3, shifts 4 right and stops at 1, giving [1, 3, 4, 9, 2]. Only the front part has been sorted so far.

questions.q: How many element shifts (piArr[j + 1] = piArr[j]) does insertion sort perform on [4, 3, 2, 1]?
questions.explain: Reverse order is the worst case: key 3 shifts 1 element, key 2 shifts 2, and key 1 shifts 3, for 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. The answer 3 counts passes, not shifts.

questions.q: Which of the two sorts from the notes is stable, keeping equal elements in their original relative order?
choices: Insertion sort, but only when sorting in descending order
Selection sort, because it makes the fewest swaps
questions.explain: Insertion sort only shifts elements that are strictly greater than the key, so equal elements never jump past each other. Selection sort's long-distance swaps can reorder equal elements.

questions.q: The input array is already sorted. How do the two sorts compare?
choices: Insertion sort does O(n) work, but selection sort still does O(n^2) comparisons
Selection sort becomes O(n), but insertion sort stays O(n^2)
questions.explain: Insertion sort's inner loop stops immediately on sorted data. Selection sort always scans the whole unsorted part to find the minimum, so it does the same work whatever order the data starts in.

questions.q: To make the course's insertion sort sort in DESCENDING order, what change is needed?
choices: Start i at iSize - 1 and count down
Change while (j >= 0 && piArr[j] > iKey) to use piArr[j] < iKey
Swap piArr[j + 1] = piArr[j] for piArr[j] = piArr[j + 1]
questions.explain: Going from ascending to descending only flips the comparison: shift while the previous element is smaller than the key. The loop structure stays the same.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of swaps selection sort makes on an array of 50 elements?
questions.explain: Selection sort does one swap per pass, and there are n - 1 passes, so 49. 1225 is the number of comparisons (49 + 48 + ... + 1), not swaps.

questions.q: Writing to storage is very expensive in your situation, so you want as few writes as possible. Which sort do the notes recommend?
choices: Either one, because they write the same amount
questions.explain: Selection sort makes at most n - 1 swaps. Insertion sort can perform many small shifts, each of which is a write.

questions.q: A student reorders the loop condition in insertion sort as shown. What is the problem?
choices: Nothing, because && checks both sides at the same time
When j reaches -1, piArr[-1] is read before j >= 0 is checked, which is out of bounds
questions.explain: && evaluates left to right and stops early, which is called short-circuiting. The original order (j >= 0 first) protects the array access, and the reordered version reads past the start of the array.

questions.q: This selection sort over Student structs compares by iID. What is wrong with its swap?
choices: swap cannot be used on ints
Nothing. Sorting by ID only needs IDs moved
Only the IDs are swapped, so names and other fields stay where they were and the records get scrambled
questions.explain: When you sort records by a key, the whole struct must move, as in swap(s[i], s[iMin]). Otherwise each ID ends up attached to the wrong student.

questions.q: How many comparisons does selection sort make on an array of 5 elements?
questions.explain: Each pass compares against every remaining element: 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10, which is n(n-1)/2. 25 (n squared) is only the rough Big-O size, not the exact count.

questions.q: New scores are added one at a time to the end of a list that is already sorted, so the list is nearly sorted. Which sort fits best?
questions.explain: On nearly sorted data, insertion sort does only a few shifts and runs close to O(n). Selection sort still does about n^2/2 comparisons.

questions.q: What is the Big-O of 3n^2 + 5n + 100?
questions.explain: Big-O drops constant factors and lower-order terms, keeping only the fastest-growing term. Writing O(3n^2) keeps a constant that Big-O ignores.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of this code?
questions.explain: These are two separate loops, one after the other, each running n times. That is 2n steps, which is O(n). Loops one after the other add, and only nested loops multiply.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of this code?
questions.explain: For each of the n values of i, the inner loop runs n times, so count++ runs n * n times.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of this code?
questions.explain: The inner loop always runs exactly 10 times, which is a constant, so the total is 10n, or O(n). As the notes point out, a nested loop does not automatically mean O(n^2).

questions.q: What is the time complexity of this loop?
questions.code:
for (int i = n; i > 1; i /= 2)
    count++;
questions.explain: i is halved on every pass, so the loop runs about log2(n) times. That is the same halving pattern that makes binary search O(log n).

questions.q: What is the time complexity of this code?
questions.explain: The outer loop runs n times. The inner j doubles each time, so it runs about log n times per outer pass. n times log n gives O(n log n).

questions.q: Which list orders the growth rates from slowest-growing to fastest-growing?
choices: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2)
O(log n), O(1), O(n), O(n^2), O(n log n)
O(1), O(log n), O(n log n), O(n), O(n^2)
O(1), O(n), O(log n), O(n^2), O(n log n)
questions.explain: Constant < logarithmic < linear < n log n < quadratic. For n = 1024, those are 1, 10, 1024, 10240 and about a million.

questions.q: For n = 64, about how many steps does an O(n log n) algorithm take?
questions.explain: log2(64) = 6, so n log n = 64 * 6 = 384. 4096 is n^2, and 6 is log n alone.

questions.q: Why does Big-O ignore constant factors such as the 5 in 5n?
choices: Computers run constants in zero time
For any fixed constant k, n^2 eventually exceeds k*n once n is large enough, so only the growth rate matters for large inputs
Constants only affect space complexity, not time
questions.explain: Big-O describes how the cost grows as n becomes large. A faster growth rate always overtakes a bigger constant, so the constant does not change the classification.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of reading arr[i] from an array?
questions.explain: Array access computes the address directly, as the start address plus i times the element size. It takes the same time whatever i or n is.

questions.q: An O(n^2) algorithm takes 1 second for n = 1000. About how long will it take for n = 2000?
questions.explain: Doubling n multiplies n^2 by 2^2 = 4. The answer 2 seconds is how a linear, O(n), algorithm would scale.

questions.q: The sorted array searched by binary search grows from 1024 to 2048 elements. How does the worst-case number of steps change?
questions.explain: log2(2048) = 11 and log2(1024) = 10. Doubling the input adds just one halving step, which is the strength of O(log n).

questions.q: Selection sort sorts the array in place, using only a few extra variables (i, j, iMin). What is its extra space complexity?
questions.explain: Space complexity counts the extra memory used. The number of extra variables does not grow with n, so it is constant, even though the time is O(n^2).

questions.q: What is the time complexity of this code?
questions.explain: The inner loop runs n, n-1, ..., 1 times, about n^2/2 in total. After dropping the constant, that is O(n^2). This is the same pattern as selection sort's comparisons.

questions.q: Which command prints the full path of your current working directory?
questions.explain: pwd stands for print working directory. ls lists the contents of a directory, cd changes directory, and man shows manual pages.

questions.q: What does g++ -Wall -o p0 test.cpp do?
choices: It compiles test.cpp with all common warnings enabled and names the executable p0
It compiles test.cpp into a.out and then runs p0
questions.explain: -Wall turns on warnings and -o names the output file. You then run the program with ./p0. Without -o, the executable would be named a.out.

questions.q: You compile with g++ test.cpp and nothing else. How do you run the result?
questions.explain: With no -o option, g++ names the executable a.out. The ./ tells the shell to look in the current directory.

questions.q: What permissions does chmod 754 file give?
questions.explain: Each digit is the sum of r = 4, w = 2 and x = 1, in the order owner, group, others. 7 = rwx, 5 = r-x and 4 = r--.

questions.q: ls -l shows -rw-r----- for a file. Which statement is correct?
choices: The group can write to it
The owner can read and write it, the group can only read it, and others have no access
questions.explain: After the leading - (regular file), the characters split into three sets: rw- for the owner, r-- for the group and --- for others. No x appears anywhere, so no one can execute it.

questions.q: Which command lists a directory's contents, including hidden files (names that start with .)?
questions.explain: Plain ls hides dotfiles, and -a means show all. ls -al combines this with the long format, which includes permissions.

questions.q: You have finished editing a file in vi. Which keys save and quit?
questions.explain: :wq means write and quit. :q! quits WITHOUT saving. Ctrl+O and Ctrl+X are nano's save and exit keys.

questions.q: What does adding -X to ssh yournetid@eros.cs.txstate.edu do?
choices: It enables X11 forwarding, so graphical programs on the server can show their windows on your machine
It runs the session as administrator
questions.explain: SSH is always encrypted. -X additionally forwards X Window graphics over that connection.

questions.q: Which command securely copies file.txt to a remote Linux host?
questions.explain: scp (secure copy) transfers files over SSH. rsync is another option. cp and mv work only on the local machine.

questions.q: A program is run as ./a.out data.txt 5. What are argc and argv[1]?
questions.explain: argc counts the program name too, so there are 3 words. argv[0] is "./a.out", so the first real argument is argv[1].

questions.q: This program is run as ./prog in.txt out.txt. What does it print?
questions.explain: argc is 3 (the program name plus two arguments), so argv[argc - 1] is argv[2], which is "out.txt". Forgetting that argv[0] is the program name leads to argc = 2.

questions.q: In the Linux file system, what is at the very top of the hierarchy, and where do users' personal directories usually live?
choices: /home is the top, with users under /root
The root directory /, with user directories under /home
~ is the top, with users under /usr
questions.explain: Linux has one tree that starts at /. Each user's home directory is normally /home/<username>, and ~ is a shortcut to your own home directory.

questions.q: Which statement about Linux's history is correct?
choices: Linux is a version of Microsoft Windows
Linux was first released as Ubuntu in 2004
Linus Torvalds introduced Linux in 1991 as a free alternative to UNIX
questions.explain: Linux is a flavor of UNIX. Ritchie created the C language in 1972, and Ubuntu (2004) is a later Linux distribution that made Linux easier to use.

questions.q: What does man pwd do?
choices: It changes into the pwd directory
It prints the current directory as the manager user
It displays the manual page for the pwd command
It makes a new directory named pwd
questions.explain: man shows the documentation for a command, including its syntax and options.

questions.q: In g++ -g -o p0 helloworld.cpp, what does -g do?
choices: It includes debugging information in the executable
It sets the name of the output file
questions.explain: -g adds debug symbols that tools such as debuggers use. -Wall enables warnings, and -o sets the output name.
